Enhanced cerebrospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy. case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

Medical history was unremarkable. She graduated from high school and worked as a driver. Smoking history and alcohol misuse were denied. One of her parents died in their late 60s with cognitive decline. On examination, her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 22, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 11. Cranial nerve tests revealed left-sided central facial palsy and lingual palsy. Pinprick sensation was decreased in the left arm. Results of other neurological or general examinations were unremarkable. The following investigations had normal or negative results: complete blood cell count, urine and stool analysis, liver and kidney function, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, blood glucose, lipids, coagulation, homocysteine, vitamins, serum tumor markers, infectious panel, lupus panel, vasculitis antibodies (anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic and anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic), and demyelination antibodies (aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein). Seventy-two–hour electrocardiography detected no atrial fibrillation. Right-side heart contrast echocardiography found no right-to-left shunts on Valsalva maneuvers. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. There were no oligoclonal bands. Enhanced cerebrospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed multifocal restricted diffusion in the corpus callosum with corresponding low apparent diffusion coefficient values (Figure, A and B). Enhanced cerebrospinal MRI showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy (Figure, C). Magnetic resonance angiography showed no atherosclerosis or stenosis.

Options:
  A. Cardiac embolism
  B. Susac syndrome
  C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
  D. Marchiafava-Bignami disease

Correct answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
